reality_anchor.topic: Why do maps look different depending on what they are made for?
evidence_claims: - The article describes that Google Maps presents multiple map representations—satellite imagery, aerial photos, street maps, 360° Street View, real-time traffic layers, and route planning—and allows users to switch among them. - It notes that the satellite view is a top-down bird’s-eye view sourced from aircraft and satellites, and that Google Maps moved from a 2D Mercator projection (which could not accurately show areas near the poles) to a 3D globe in 2018, with an option to switch back to 2D.

The authors describe constructing a full-sky 100 μm map by combining COBE/DIRBE and IRAS/ISSA data and explicitly removing zodiacal light, confirmed point sources, and IRAS scan artifacts to isolate Galactic dust emission. They use DIRBE 100 and 240 μm data to build a dust temperature map so the 100 μm brightness can be converted to a quantity proportional to dust column density, noting that temperature variations can change the inferred column by a factor of five. They say the map’s primary use is estimating Galactic extinction and calibrate it using colors of elliptical galaxies, while also noting applications for predicting millimeter foregrounds in CMB experiments and soft X-ray absorption. They report achieving DIRBE-quality calibration with IRAS resolution and handle zodiacal and possible cosmic infrared background components via regression and wavelength-dependent treatment.
